This 1990 Ex-Military Truck Is Now a Massive Expedition RV for Daring Adventurers
29 photos
Photo: Bring a Trailer
There are expedition campers, and then there are expedition campers built on former military trucks. For overlanders looking for a go-anywhere off-road expedition vehicle, ex-army trucks have always carried a special appeal. Not because they are fashionable, but because they’re incredibly capable and let you easily access any destination you have in mind.
This 1990 BMY M931A2 6×6 ex-military truck that has been turned into a capable camper for daring adventurers shows why these vehicles have always had a place in the overland world. Designed for demanding environments, with unbeatable durability and strength, this vehicle was originally designed to haul heavy loads for the U.S. Army. It was transformed into a full-fledged expedition motorhome by Plan B Trucks of Utah in 2017 and is a great rig for adventurers who don’t like getting stuck in mud or snow.
At 36 feet (nearly 11 meters) long, this is a massive motorhome with the road manners typically associated with military vehicles. However, it combines the serious expedition capability with a surprisingly comfortable living space with an open floor plan, practical amenities, and the equipment needed for extended trips away from home.
Built in Ohio by Bowen-McLaughlin-York (BMY), a division of Harsco Corporation, the M931A2 is a heavy-duty, five-ton tactical semi-tractor truck that was part of the U.S. Army’s M939 series of trucks. It was designed specifically to haul semi-trailers across difficult military environments and rough terrain.
Photo: Bring a Trailer The A2 model, manufactured for just a few years, from 1989 to 1992, introduced a series of enhancements meant to increase reliability and performance. These included a turbocharged Cummins diesel engine and a central tire inflation system. Plan B Trucks kept the original mechanical setup when converting the particular A2 truck featured here, preserving much of its capability and military character.
This means power comes from an 8.3-liter Cummins 6CTA turbodiesel inline-six producing 240 hp and 745 lb-ft of torque. The powerful mill is paired with an Allison five-speed automatic transmission and a Rockwell dual-range transfer case, which sends power to the rear wheels or all six wheels as needed. Rockwell axles and air brakes complete the heavy-duty drivetrain.
The team at Plan B outfitted the BMY M931A2 with a purpose-built habitation box that offers approximately 27 feet (8.2 meters) of interior length and includes all the essential amenities for comfortable on-the-road journeys.
Photo: Bring a Trailer The exterior of this expedition machine is finished in red and black bedliner material, giving the vehicle a rugged appearance. At the front, it features a huge steel bumper with an electric winch rated at 17,500 pounds, and on the roof, it has nine solar panels. Plan B also added LED lighting, several storage compartments, and a powered awning on the side for a shaded outdoor area. Utility connections for water and electricity and a pintle hitch for towing complete the exterior setup.
For the interior living quarters, they used wood-paneled walls and flooring to create a warmer, more welcoming ambiance than the rugged exterior might suggest. The floor plan includes a rear U-shaped dinette, a small lounge with a sofa and swing-out TV, a full kitchen, and wet and dry bathroom areas. The rig also integrates multiple sleeping areas, including a queen-size overcab bed, a drop-down bed above the dinette, and a fold-out sofa, which means it can sleep a whole family or group of friends.
Photo: Bring a Trailer The rear dinette comes with red upholstered benches and a wooden table, providing a nice seating area for dining or hanging out. The fold-down sofa provides another place to relax, while the galley is equipped for serious cooking sessions. It features stainless-steel countertops, a sink, a two-burner induction cooktop, a microwave, and a refrigerator/freezer.
The bathroom is split into two separate areas. The wet section has a shower with a handheld sprayer, while the dry bathroom contains a sink and toilet. Storage cabinets are integrated where possible, providing plenty of room for the travelers’ belongings, and a gun safe is also included.
The expedition truck camper is designed to offer comfort in any season, with a 14,000-BTU air conditioner and a diesel-powered heater keeping the interior comfortable in different weather conditions. The electrical system is designed for off-grid travel, with solar panels, charge controllers, lithium house batteries, and a Xantrex inverter.
Photo: Bring a Trailer The rig carries two 125-gallon (473-liter) freshwater tanks, as well as separate 45-gallon (170-liter) gray-water and 45-gallon (170-liter) black-water tanks. The fuel capacity is also substantial thanks to two 75-gallon (284-liter) diesel tanks, which translates into long journeys between refills.
This beast of a camper was featured on the television series Extreme RVs in 2017. It has covered around 22,000 miles so far, and its engine was reportedly overhauled in 2008, while it was still in military service. The house batteries were also replaced recently, and all eight wheels received new Goodyear 395/85R20 MV/T tires this year.
Though not as shiny as a new build, this rig carries history, purpose, and a certain charm that you rarely get with other expedition vehicles. The BMY M931A2 truck camper was recently offered for sale through Bring a Trailer, but the auction ended without a sale because the reserve was not met.

2029 Porsche Macan ICE Test Mule Grows Custom Front End
43 photos
Photo: Baldauf
The newest internal combustion Porsche Macan test mule shows how far project Octan has moved beyond the Q5 donor. While this fellow may use plenty of Audi-sourced panels, the custom front end, widened fenders, and prominent quad exhaust outlets point to a very different animal from the Q5. Due in 2028, the next-gen Macan is based on the Premium Platform Combustion and is likely to feature Q5 powertrains as well.
Expected to hit American showrooms as a 2029 model, the next iteration of the Macan is still far from revealing its production-intent bodywork and signature lighting. The Audi origins are obvious here, and naysayers are wrong in criticizing Porsche for this choice because the original Macan was also twinned with the Q5 from that era.
Instead of just another 2026 model year Q5, the mule had its nose altered with a custom bumper with large openings for the radiators. Their dimensions indicate turbocharged gasoline options, and plug-in hybrid assistance is a given as well. White foam blocks underneath may look odd, but said blocks are there for measuring ground clearance on the track.
Think of them as a useful early-stage check for the chassis and suspension setup before Porsche fits the final bodywork and related componentry. The wider stance of the Macan also differentiates it from the Q5 and SQ5, although spy photos of near-production RS Q5 prototypes indicate that Audi can also play the width card.
Wider tracks don't automatically make a car faster, but going wide makes a world of difference in the corners. The larger contact patch of a wider tire further supports acceleration and deceleration, whereas the more planted look should be viewed as the cherry on top.
Photo: Baldauf Interior photos of the 2029 model year Macan do not exist as of this writing. Even so, it's easy to imagine a Q5 interior with a bit of Porsche magic here and there. Whether the Flow Display of the Cayenne Electric will also make the cut, that remains to be seen. Porsche's own strategy material has confirmed gasoline and plug-in hybrid powertrains, yet Porsche has not mentioned whether four cylinders are in the offing as well.
The 3.0-liter turbo V6 of the SQ5 seems most appropriate for this application, and the same can be said about the 2.9-liter twin-turbo V6 of the RS Q5 for the most performance-oriented Macan of them all. Shared with the RS 5, the plug-in hybrid sixer of the RS Q5 is expected to generate the very same 630 horsepower and 609 pound-feet (825 Newton-meters).
As for the SQ5, which is mild hybrid in Europe and completely internal combustion in the United States, the numbers are 362 horsepower and 406 pound-feet (550 Newton-meters). Audi calls the mild-hybrid system MHEV Plus, and the 48-volt system is built around a permanently excited synchronous motor that is mounted to the transmission's output shaft.
Audi refers to it as the powertrain generator, and this unit can perform low-speed maneuvers solely on electric power. In coasting mode, the electric motor does its thing at speeds no higher than 86 mph (140 kph). Beyond said motor, a smaller one is used by the belt alternator starter.
The harsh reality is that the old Macan will have been out of production for roughly two years by the time the new one shows up. Dealers will have to bridge that period with the Macan Electric, which isn't as big of a commercial success as the internal combustion model was during its final years.

With the more than 2,200 comments filed to the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration are overwhelmingly in favor of codifying current regulations on English Language Proficiency (ELP), the few urging caution tend to stick out.
That is particularly true in the case of the Sikh Coalition, which is not a trucking-specific organization but one that given the large number of Sikh drivers on U.S. highways has taken particular interest in the ELP regulation.
The Sikh Coalition, in its comments filed to FMCSA, described itself as a “nonprofit and nonpartisan organization dedicated to ensuring that members of the Sikh community in America are able to practice their faith without fear of discrimination or backlash.”
Its description of the organization goes on to say that the group “(defends) the civil rights and civil liberties of Sikhs, including Sikh truck drivers, by providing direct legal services, advocating for legislative change, educating the public about Sikhs and Sikhi, and fostering civic engagement amongst Sikh Americans.”
The Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) on ELP took comments through last Friday. The proposed rule “would make updates,” according to the NPRM, to various existing regulations to “reflect that noncompliance with ELP requirements will result in a driver being placed out of service.”
The one exception would be truck traffic localized to the U.S.-Mexico border that wasn’t heading further inland.
Supporters mount email campaign
The largest source of comments submitted to FMCSA was through a campaign from an unknown organizer in support of the proposed rule. It manifested itself in the form of verbatim submissions by dozens of individuals that raised the story of Dalilah Coleman.
Dalilah Coleman was five when she was injured in a 2024 crash in California involving a driver in the U.S. illegally.
The email comments from that lobbying drive all opened with the same wording.
“Dalilah’s story should not be the next in a saga of many others like it,” the emails said. “It should be the last one ever told. The illegal alien driving that truck should never have been allowed behind the wheel.”
That crash led to the introduction of Dalilah’s Law in the House of Representatives and the Senate. Its provisions include ELP requirements.
While the House of Representatives” Committee on Transportation & Infrastructure voted to advance the bill , it has not been taken up by the full House . Its Senate companion did not get a vote in the corresponding committee.
Given the calendar, passage of Dalilah’s Law is unlikely to occur this year. It would need to be considered by the next Congress to become law.
Concerns about discrimination
In its comment to FMCSA, the Sikh Coalition said it “(agrees) there is a common-sense safety need for all drivers to understand a level of English as is already required by federal law.” But it added that “certain steps needed to be taken to mitigate the risk of discrimination during the course of or under the guise of ELP enforcement.”
The Coalition said in earlier communications with the Department of Transportation , it had “raised concerns” about several issues, including what it said was “the lack of clear criteria for roadside inspectors to use to determine whether to subject drivers to ELP assessments, and the lack of any information as to what recourse is available to drivers rendered out of service (OOS) due to alleged ELP violations.”
It cited a FMCSA decision from 2016 that the agency “had previously removed the requirement to place drivers out-of-service because the Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance could not substantiate the safety impact of the requirement.”
The Coalition also said it had communicated to FMCSA that the Sikhs’ analysis of FMCSA data on roadside inspections between 2021 and 2025 showed that just 0.19% “involved a driver’s inability to communicate in or understand English.”
ELP was a Road Check focus
However, this year’s Road Check Week resulted in EPL violations becoming a top 5 reason for inspectors to hand down an OOS order. ELP violations consisted of 9.1% of all OOS orders.
“Our goal is to reduce the risk of any discrimination against truck drivers who could
be profiled for their appearance and subject to disproportionate or discriminatory
additional scrutiny during roadside inspections in the name of ELP enforcement,” the Sikh Coalition comments said. “It is critical that FMCSA establish clear, objective standards for roadside inspectors tasked with carrying out ELP enforcement to mitigate the risk of wrongful discrimination against Sikh or other commercial drivers.”
The Coalition’s comments also raise the social media post posted last month by the Department of Homeland Security– later taken down –that made reference to Sikh drivers and declared “Get off our roads, you don’t know how to drive, Mr. Singh.”
“FMCSA has consistently provided reason to believe that it is less interested in improving safety outcomes and more interested in removing certain drivers from the road because of where they come from,” the Coalition’s comments said.
It wrapped up its comments by asking FMCSA to withdraw the NPRM, and “instead invest in tailored, evidence-based safety measures.”
The key U.S. trucking organizations, in their comments, broadly backed the goals of the ELP rule. But there were recommendations for some changes.
ATA’s concerns
The American Trucking Associations , in a comment that seemed to indirectly echo the Sikh Coalition’s criticism that the ELP/OOS criteria could be vague, said the ATA “remains concerned that the current assessment process leaves room for subjective interpretation by individual enforcement officials.”
“Without standardized scoring metrics or clearly defined evaluation criteria, ELP determinations may vary considerably from one roadside inspection to another,” the ATA said. “For example, a driver’s level of English proficiency may be deemed sufficient by one officer yet insufficient by another based on differing interpretations of the same interaction.”
ATA called on FMCSA to work with the states issuing CDLs “to establish and build in a standardized ELP assessment as part of the CDL issuance and renewal process.”
“Doing so would help evaluate and catch drivers with ELP deficiencies at ‘the front door’ – ensuring drivers are tested for ELP based on a consistent national standard before receiving a credential to operate, rather than relying primarily on roadside inspections to identify deficiencies after a driver has entered the workforce.”
The Owner Operator Independent Drivers Association ’s (OOIDA) comments had few recommendations and was more effusive in its praise than ATA.
But it did add a history of earlier enforcement action.
It said that CVSA removed an ELP requirement in 2015. After that, OOIDA wrote, “ELP violations went largely unenforced and unreported for a decade.”
“In 2014, there were over 100,000 ELP violations at roadside; yet in 2024, there were just 9,700 ELP violations reported,” OOIDA said. “The lack of ELP enforcement, in conjunction with the growth of States issuing Non-Domiciled Commercial Driver s Licenses to foreign drivers during the same period, permitted hundreds of thousands of unqualified drivers to work on our nation’s roads. This needlessly resulted in numerous fatal crashes.”

LEGO Ideas Interstellar Endurance Would Shame Even the Largest Space-Related Sets
9 photos
Photo: LEGO/GMB29
Christopher Nolan's 2014 Interstellar movie will forever remain in the minds of all sci-fi lovers out there as one of the most scientifically grounded works in the history of filmmaking. Far from being a sci-fi work that involves huge space battles and lasers, it has everything it needs to become a reference point in Hollywood history.
We’ve got a sentient species in danger of extinction on a dying Earth, spacecraft being built to find a way out of the corner humanity pushed itself into, space travel and AI, and black holes with all the nasty things that come with them, including huge gravity pull and time dilation.
On the off chance you haven’t seen the flick yet, I won’t spoil it for you. For the purpose of our story here, suffice to say that NASA’s in-movie efforts to ensure a future for the human race involve sending a spacecraft to a supermassive black hole called Gargantua.
The object in question is called Endurance, an interplanetary spacecraft shaped like a ring that measures 210 feet (64 meters) in diameter. Its goal is to transport a crew of four people and two oddly shaped robots on a mission to rescue the crew of a previous mission and the future of humanity.
In the grand scheme of things, the ship doesn’t necessarily play a big role in the movie, as it’s only used to transport the crew, carry a pair of smaller spacecraft called Ranger and Lander, and is involved, but only marginally so, in some of the film's most intense scenes.
That didn’t stop a LEGO fan designer who goes by the name GMB29 on LEGO Ideas from imagining a 1:123 scale replica of the Endurance. And I must admit, the thing looks like it would be an amazing addition to any Interstellar fan collection.
We’re not told how many LEGO parts went into designing the set, but the interesting part about it is that it comes complete with two Lander and Ranger spacecraft, just like in the movie. They are detachable, so some of the movie’s most iconic scenes could be recreated, and they can be attached to the ring in a very simple fashion.
The set, which is presently listed on LEGO Ideas, also includes minifigures of the crew: we’ve got Joseph Cooper, Amelia Brand, Romilly, Doyle, and even Dr. Mann. Why, even the box-shaped TARS robot is included. The set has been imagined with a stand, so that it could be properly displayed.
The LEGO Ideas Endurance was submitted for public voting at the end of April, and it presently has 1,772 backers and no less than 440 days to reach 5,000. If it does that, the set would get another extension to reach 10,000 supporters and be officially considered for production by the Danish toy maker.

Have You Seen One? 1960 Dodge Polara Hardtop Wagon Is Probably the Finest Still Around
10 photos
Photo: Charles Phoenix/YouTube
Built from 1960 to 1973, the Polara is not one of Dodge's longest-running nameplates. However, it's one of the brand's most iconic. But not all iterations of the premium model get attention from collectors nowadays.
The 1962-1964 version has a solid following today. The Polara produced during this period competed in the mid-size segment. It was among the first Mopars produced on the B-body platform and one of Dodge's earliest muscle cars. Chrysler had yet to launch the 426 Hemi, but the Polara was available with the equally spectacular Max Wedge V8.
Then we have the Polara built from 1965 onward. This version was a full-size car and rode on the larger C-body platform. It was massive, stylish, and available with high-performance engines. The two-door versions are relatively sought-after, albeit not very expensive.
As for the early Polara produced in 1960-1961, which is also a full-size model, it's largely ignored. And that's mainly due to the polarizing design. Early 1960s Dodges are widely regarded as ugly, although some find them rather bold. I actually like these cars, and I'm particularly fond of the 1960 variant.
And that's precisely why I'm showing you this station wagon. This and the fact that it's also a rare sight. Not necessarily by production numbers, but because many of them have morphed into rust buckets in junkyards and barns . Unlike its siblings, this grocery-getter is in pristine condition.
1960 was the first year for the Polara. It replaced the Coronet and topped a full-size car lineup that also included the entry-level Dart and the mid-range Matador. Much like its predecessor, the Polara came in various shapes, including a four-door sedan, a four-door hardtop, a two-door hardtop, and a two-door convertible.
However, Dodge also offered a rather quirky four-door hardtop station wagon. Yup, for a short period of time, some automakers experimented with pillarless grocery-getters. The hardtop version was exclusive to the Polara line; it was not available on the Dart and Matador.
The Polara was somewhat popular in 1960, moving 42,517 units (11% of the entire Dodge production output). However, the hardtop wagon didn't find many customers: only 3,004 examples rolled off the assembly line. This figure included 1,236 six-passenger cars and 1,768 nine-passenger (three-row) vehicles.
The main culprit for the low sales was the asking price. The six-passenger version started from $3,506 ($40,300 in 2026 dollars), a 30% premium over the standard Dart Seneca wagon. It was also about 9% pricier than the Matador. The nine-passenger version came in at $3,620 but could cost as much as $4,200 ($48,300 in 2026 dollars) with certain options.
This wagon is one of the 1,768 three-row models sold that year, and it's downright stunning. It's unclear if it's a restoration or a well-maintained survivor, but it doesn't matter all that much. The fact that it looks showroom-new is both rare and outstanding. And make sure you check them angled rear wings. While it may not be beautiful in the conventional sense, this Polara is pretty flamboyant.
How many of these wagons are still around? Well, I've only seen a couple cross the auction block in recent years. And back in 2020, a pristine example that was estimated to sell for $40,000 to $55,000 fetched a whopping $93,500. Hit the play button below to check this one out.

She Kept Grandpa's 1972 Ford F-100 Parked for over 20 Years, Sells It for $2,000
15 photos
Photo: Chase Gentry | YouTube
This 1972 Ford F-100 spent over 20 long years parked in its owner's backyard after many years and miles on the road, all with the same family. They finally decided to list it for sale. The one who took it home found the truck on Facebook Marketplace and drove 11 hours to check it out, not sure if he would go back home with the F-100.
Off-road enthusiast Chase Gentry was scrolling on Facebook Marketplace in search of a truck when he laid his eyes on a 1972 Ford F-100 Sport Custom and felt that it was the one. The seller was asking $3,000 to let it go. He instantly messaged the owner to ask if he could do $2,000. " Yes, sure can ," he immediately replied.
So Chase packed his things, took his Ford F-150 Raptor R and his trailer, and started his 760-mile, 11-hour-long trip from his home in Harlingen to Amarillo, Texas, not knowing what he would find. He considered the worst-case scenarios: a rusted frame, the owner changing his mind. It can't possibly be easy to let go of a truck that has been with the family for 54 years. What else could go wrong?
The current owner of the truck, Linda, welcomes him in the driveway and tells him it was the truck on which she learned how to drive. Actually, she was too small to reach the pedals, so Grandpa sat her on his lap, controlling the pedals, while steering was all she did.
Photo: Chase Gentry | YouTube Grandpa was actually the original owner of the Ford F-100. He drove it off the showroom floor in 1972, and it was his workhorse, but also his pride and joy up until he handed it out to Linda's father. But then, life happened, and her father parked it in the backyard in 2005 and never touched it again.
That is exactly where Chase finds it, covered in dust and grime, with the interior in black and white, mirroring over two decades of neglect. He pops the hood to see what is underneath. The engine bay must have been a playground for the mice that chewed hoses and wires and everything they found edible by mouse standards.
Linda has no idea what engine powers the truck, but takes a wild guess at a 360-cubic-inch V8. Back in the day, the lineup started with the base 240 CID inline-six with 121 horsepower (123 metric horsepower), while the 390-cubic-inch V8 sat at the top of the lineup with 201 horsepower (204 metric horsepower). The 360 was the second most powerful variant available, pushing out 196 horsepower (199 metric horsepower).
Luckily, the $2,000 deal is still standing, so Chase is buying it and naming it Sheila, after their lab that has recently passed away. He has been dreaming of owning a yellow F-100 for years. The 1972 model year was the sixth and final year of the fifth-generation Ford F-Series.
Photo: Chase Gentry | YouTube Famously known by truck enthusiasts as the Bumpside generation due to the distinct, convex body crease running along the sides, the 1972 model was a transition year right before Ford debuted the Dentside sixth-generation model in 1973.
Chase tows his all-new old F-100 out of its entrapment with the help of his F-150 Raptor R and loads it onto the trailer, well aware that the truck is not just one more project but a vehicle with a story, which spent half a century with the same family. Chase grinned with joy all the way home, ten hours long.
$2,000, 22 hours on the road, and a wash later, the new owner is surprised to see the truck is in better condition than he expected. The yellow paint is immaculate, despite the fact that the truck spent 20 years parked in the sun. But to get it looking this clean, he had to deal with mouse nests. It took him four days to clean it up.
The original bench seat has the upholstery cut open, so he will have to solve that issue, too. Everything is original in and out, just like it was back in 1972. He will also have to come up with a solution to the surface rust in the load bed. Despite all of the issues the 54-year-old Ford came with, it was too good of a deal to turn around and walk away.
Photo: Chase Gentry | YouTube Chase paid less than what buyers used to pay for a new truck in 1972, when it started at $2,521. Adjusted for inflation, that original base price translates to roughly $18,800 in today's money. There is no truck on the American market retailing that low nowadays. Even the Slate Truck is about $6,000 more expensive.
From this moment on, Chase has two options: either fully restore it or keep the patina and work on the internals to make it run and drive properly. He loves the patina, so the original paint is staying. But he wouldn't really mind an engine swap and 500 horsepower.

The winter equipment experts at Prinoth are partnering with Swedish trucking group SCANIA on a pair of new, battery-electric snow groomers that are ready to hit Europe’s ski slopes with up to 624 kWh of battery power all winter long.
You read that right. Scania will provide Prinoth with its in-house Core 800 li-ion battery system – a 691V solution that includes integrated liquid cooling and a proprietary charging management system that’s built around energy-dense battery packs that are meant to be modular and scalable from just 21 kWh all the way up to a whopping 624 kWh. More than enough, in other words, to keep carving fresh corduroy long after the lifts start spinning.
“Collaborating with Prinoth is an exciting challenge for us, as it involves deploying our battery technology in extremely demanding conditions,” says Elin Åkerström, Managing Director, Scania Industrial Batteries. “Snow groomers operate in very low temperatures and steep terrain, moving heavy volumes of snow. This requires batteries that can deliver high power, withstand cold climates, and handle vibrations. We are proud that our technology has been recognized through this long-term agreement.”
The machines in question are an electrified version of the Prinoth Husky and the recently announced Leitwolf E-Motion, which places the Scania Core 800 battery packs in both top and side orientations to meet higher energy and power requirements, further expanding the available use cases for the brand’s heavy-duty snow groomers.

"Mother-in-Law Drove It to High School": 1962 Chevrolet Needs Restoration, So Cheap
24 photos
Photo: eBay seller tonysrodz
My mother-in-law drove this car to high-school. This is how the owner describes this 1962 Chevrolet Impala that now needs a complete restoration.
This Impala is not the most solid restoration candidate, but on the other hand, it’s not a wreck either. Bringing it back to the road should be quite cheap, and one of the most important things is that it’s quite affordable.
Before I delve into more details, it’s important to know that the car is no longer original. The floors have already been replaced long ago, possibly as the Impala received another partial refresh. That’s why, if you’re interested in buying the car, arranging an in-person inspection is probably the best thing you can do before making an offer.
Photo: eBay seller tonysrodz The Impala was already the best-selling car in the United States in 1962, and the full-size lineup was the one keeping Chevrolet at the top of the charts.
The GM brand ended the year with 2.1 million cars, and the full-size series accounted for over 1.4 million units. The Impala was the top model with over 700,000 buyers, followed by the Bel Air and the Biscayne.
1962 was the second year for the Super Sport , but otherwise, the engine lineup continued to include a mix of six-cylinder units and V8s. The base engine was a 235 rated at 135 horsepower, while the standard V8 was the 283 two-barrel rated at 170 horsepower.
The 327 was a new engine and allowed users to step into the small-block space with a 250 horsepower unit that included a four-barrel carburetor and a dual-exhaust system. For $245 more, buyers could get the 300-horsepower version.
The 409 was the top choice this year. This big-block Turbo-Fire could be had with 380 horsepower, but if money wasn’t an issue and customers agreed to pay $484, they could get a 409-horsepower configuration with dual four-barrel carburetors, a high-light cam, and solid lifters.
Photo: eBay seller tonysrodz It goes without saying that the big-block specimens are the most desirable today, so you might end up disappointed by this car. It’s because it’s fitted with a six-cylinder engine, though it’s unclear if this is the original unit.
The 235 is paired with a Powerglide transmission, and the seller reveals in their post that it starts, runs, and drives great. This is good news for someone who wants a regular driver, as this Impala already seems prepared for a short journey.
Sure, it has clearly seen better days, but considering its mechanical condition, taking the car on a short trip should be doable.
However, you shouldn’t assume that this Impala doesn’t need anything. It does, and this is the most obvious once you open the driver’s door and step inside. The interior needs a complete refresh, and the seller is honest and admits that major work is required in the cabin.
The same on the body, though I must admit that I’ve seen cars in worse shape getting fixed, so I see no reason why this Impala wouldn’t return to the road.
Photo: eBay seller tonysrodz The seller explains that this Impala was originally used by his mother in law to go to high-school back in the day. This makes sense, considering it’s fitted with a 235, as this unit was considered one of the most efficient - and also the most reliable - daily driver. It didn’t burn as much fuel as a V8 and didn’t require costly repairs in the long term.
Otherwise, it’s hard to find a reason to walk away, especially if you know what to expect. I believe it’s important to understand that this car is not supposed to be a collectible but just an honest restoration project that can easily become a father-son mission. This car can easily become a daily driver, though I think it’s essential that you get more specifics to know precisely how much you;ll end up spending on the project.
The owner is realistic, and this is why I expect this Impala to find a new home quite fast.
Photo: eBay seller tonysrodz The seller is willing to let this Impala go for no more, no less than $4,000, which is a fantastic price for a car that you can restore without spending high dollars. 1962 full-size Chevrolet donors are easy to find, especially because the Impala shares the metal and many other parts with more affordable siblings like the Bel Air and the Biscayne, so bringing this car back to the road shouldn’t be costly.
The owner also enabled the Make Offer option, meaning that you might get an even better deal if you’re committed to a purchase. Just use this button if you want the car and have another deal in mind.
You’ll have to pick up the car from Sullivan, Indiana, and considering it’s in good shape, you might be able to take it home on its wheels if the journey back to your garage doesn’t involve a long journey.

source_document.body:
AI gets plenty of attention, but some of the work needed to make it useful gets less discussion. At o9 Solutions’ aim10x Americas event in Chicago last month, Supply Chain 24/7 asked five executives the same question: What aren’t people talking enough about?
What’s Related
Their answers ranged from how planners will navigate new software to how companies will apply lessons from past decisions to their next plan. Here are the issues they believe deserve more attention.
1. Simon Joiner, o9 : Helping planners navigate a new way of working
A system that lets planners ask any question sounds appealing. But familiar screens and workflows also help people track which steps they have completed, said Simon Joiner, o9’s director of product management.
“What have you done and what haven’t you done? How do you know where you are?” he asked.
Joiner said companies need to test how conversational tools and traditional workflows will work together, using real employees, data , and processes. He expects that testing to help determine whether planners still need established workflows or a different way of working.
“What have you done and what haven’t you done? How do you know where you are?”
— Simon Joiner
“I think we’re going to have to do it in phases,” he said.
He described offering traditional tools enhanced with AI alongside more AI-driven options. Customers are at different stages, he said, so they will need different ways to use the software during the transition.
2. Marie Fodness, WHOOP : Teaching employees what happens behind an AI answer
Marie Fodness, WHOOP’s AVP of global operations, said employees using AI need to understand the calculations being performed and the data and sources behind the analysis. Her team uses lunch-and-learns and other sessions to help build that understanding.
“I don’t think we talk enough about what that looks like for the individual contributor, in the lower-level job function, day to day,” she said.
Fodness wants employees to explain the data and understand what an AI model is doing. That means giving them resources and time to learn about the analysis they increasingly hand off to these tools.
“It definitely slides under the radar,” she said.
MORE FROM THE O9 CONFERENCE: Six Things to Consider Before Buying Planning Software | How the Micah Parsons Trade Helped Shape Fanatics’ Inventory Plans
3. Igor Rikalo, o9 : Putting lessons from past decisions into the next plan
Companies often review decisions after a major event, but those reviews can take considerable time, said Igor Rikalo, o9’s president and COO. The lessons may then remain outside the planning system rather than become part of the next planning or execution cycle.
Rikalo described the manual work of assembling a team, collecting data, and analyzing what happened. He estimated that automating that work could save a few weeks and reduce involvement to roughly a dozen people.
The goal is to collect the information needed to explain what happened, analyze it, and produce a report showing what the company could have done differently. Those findings then need to feed into the next cycle.
“How do we create processes inside of the companies to actually capture the richness of the context around the decisions to be able to learn?” he asked.
“How do we create processes inside of the companies to actually capture the richness of the context around the decisions to be able to learn?”
— Igor Rikalo
4. Amit Shah, Acuity Brands: Revisiting improvements that once cost too much
Amit Shah, product manager, supply chain planning at Acuity Brands, said faster computing makes smaller planning improvements worth another look. He illustrated the opportunity with moving “from a 90% optimized answer to a 94% optimized answer.”
“In the past, that 4% was meaningless because the cost to get that was very, very large,” he said.
Shah was describing an example of the opportunity, rather than reporting a measured result at Acuity. His point was that the work required to find a better answer can now be lower, making improvements more economical to pursue.
He sees an underused opportunity in making small gains more efficiently that eventually add up to something larger. That includes revisiting improvements whose cost previously outweighed their benefit.
5. Brent Hasenkamp, o9: Helping internal teams implement and change systems
Much of the AI discussion focuses on what companies can do once a system is running. Brent Hasenkamp, o9’s SVP of sales for North America, said AI also offers a way to shorten the work of connecting data and configuring software.
“AI has really enabled us to do integration so much faster, configuration so much faster,” he said.
Hasenkamp also described using AI to compare plans with actual results and identify where they differ. Beyond speeding implementation, he sees an opportunity for companies’ internal teams to make changes with less specialized technical expertise.
With an internal center of excellence working with o9’s AI tools, he said employees would not have to be “the most tech-savvy solution architect, strategist, configuration person” to make a change.

source_document.body:
Japan will provide up to $21 billion for two planned chip factories at GlobalFoundries’ site in Malta, New York, with the first expected to begin operating in 2029. GlobalFoundries will run the factories and provide the technology used to manufacture its chips.
The company’s Oct. 14 announcement outlines about $10 billion in initial investment for the first factory, with another roughly $10 billion contemplated for the second. The project is part of a U.S.-Japan trade and investment agreement and will serve automotive , industrial, and connected infrastructure customers.
GlobalFoundries expects to break ground on the first factory later this year. The Malta site already has permits, and construction will use existing infrastructure.
When fully operational, the first factory is expected to produce approximately 900,000 300mm wafers annually. Each wafer is a circular sheet of silicon, about 12 inches wide, on which many individual chips are made.
The project is expected to create more than 1,000 manufacturing jobs and about 27,000 construction and related jobs in New York’s Capital Region.
RELATED: GlobalFoundries to Invest $16B in NY and Vermont Chip Plants
How the factories will be run
Japan will supply all investment capital, while U.S. and Japanese interests will jointly own the factories, Reuters reported. GlobalFoundries will earn fees for construction, operations and licensing its chip manufacturing technology.
CEO Tim Breen told Reuters that GlobalFoundries would manage customer relationships, with Apple and Japan’s Renesas Electronics among the initial customers.
“We definitely would like to give priority to US and Japanese customers,” he said.
Customers plan for more U.S. chip supply
Renesas said it is planning around the new factories as an extension of its own production. The company tied the additional supply to demand for electrification, connectivity, AI, and data center equipment.
“This expanded collaboration further strengthens the stable, long-term supply of semiconductors with the differentiated technologies, quality and reliability our products require,” said Renesas CEO Hidetoshi Shibata.
Cirrus Logic also said the factories would give it access to U.S. manufacturing for future chips that process both analog and digital signals. Tokyo Electron, a supplier of chipmaking equipment, said it plans to contribute to the U.S. expansion after years of working with GlobalFoundries.
Separate funding for New York and Vermont
GlobalFoundries also agreed with the U.S. Department of Commerce to redirect $955 million from its existing CHIPS and Science Act award toward investments in Malta and Burlington, Vermont. Those projects will expand manufacturing for communications infrastructure and data centers.
The work includes silicon photonics, which uses light to move data, silicon-germanium technology, and advanced packaging , which connects chip components. In a separate agreement, Commerce will receive an approximately 4% equity stake in GlobalFoundries.

Waabi and Warrior Logistics announced a commercial partnership Wednesday to move routine customer freight on Waabi Driver-powered autonomous trucks between Dallas and Houston. Warrior, an asset-based carrier headquartered in Coppell, Texas , has added a fleet of Waabi’s trucks to its network to haul recurring shipments for food and beverage, consumer goods and other customers.
The companies began commercial operations earlier this year. Routes completed by the autonomous trucks since then have produced 100% on-time pickup and delivery and zero safety incidents, according to Waabi . Neither company disclosed how many Waabi trucks Warrior runs or how many loads they have hauled.
The carrier, founded in 2015, runs more than 200 trucks of its own, according to the companies’ release . It is using the Waabi trucks to add capacity and raise utilization across that broader fleet as customer demand grows.
“Our customers want more capacity on our core lanes, and they want it to be consistent,” said Scott McFarlane, CEO of Warrior Logistics. “Our partnership with Waabi gives us the flexibility to deliver that. Waabi Driver-powered trucks complement our professional drivers, build density on our power lanes, and add capacity on the routes that are less desirable for our drivers.”
McFarlane described a network where autonomous trucks and professional drivers run side by side. That mix lets Warrior take on more freight and keep its drivers on the lanes they want to run, he said.
Why Warrior signed on
Warrior began the partnership for three reasons, McFarlane said: a leadership team it trusts, technology he called truly innovative and a co-development approach that let the carrier see firsthand how safely the Waabi Driver performs.
“The results on our own freight speak for themselves,” he said.
“Warrior has helped shape our technology over the course of our partnership and the impact we’re seeing across their operations shows how we can help carriers take on more freight, serve more customers and grow their business,” said Lior Ron, COO of Waabi.
Over the coming year, the two companies will jointly pick and develop the next lanes for the autonomous trucks across Warrior’s network.
Waabi’s Dallas-Houston business
The Warrior deal comes nine days after Waabi and Volvo Autonomous Solutions began hauling freight for Warp , their first customer operation together. Volvo VNL Autonomous trucks running the Waabi Driver move Warp freight directly to third-party facilities on the same corridor, with an observer in the driver’s seat.
Commercial load volume on Waabi’s Dallas-Houston route has grown more than 80% this year, the company said. It did not give a baseline.
Its first revenue loads on Interstate 45 between Dallas and Houston moved in September 2023, the week it announced a 10-year deal with Uber Freight .
In July, Waabi said its software, trained only on a Peterbilt 579, drove a Volvo VNL Autonomous truck with no new data or fine-tuning.
Waabi’s trucks are not yet driverless. Ron told FreightWave s in January the company will remove the driver only once the truck and its fully redundant platform are ready from the manufacturer.
This month, he said Waabi is “fully on track for driverless next year, with Volvo as the first OEM platform.”

1967 Hemi GTX Needs Nothing but a New Set of Hands on the Wheel, the Low Mileage Has History
24 photos
Photo: Craigslist
The 1967 Plymouth GTX was Chrysler's brilliant answer to a booming muscle car market. Conceived as a gentleman's hot rod, this absolute beauty combined upscale luxury features with brutal, unrelenting street performance. It was essentially the Plymouth equivalent of the Dodge Coronet R/T, offering eager buyers the exact same potent powertrain combinations.
Chrysler clearly wanted to attract a slightly more mature crowd that secretly longed blistering acceleration without sacrificing everyday driving comfort.
Hitting dealership floors in the fall of 1966 for the 1967 model year, the Plymouth GTX rode on the proven B-body platform shared with the Belvedere and Satellite. In fact, the famous three-letter acronym piggybacked the Belvedere in its debut season, but was quickly set free as a separate series, in 1968.
Plymouth kept things simple and straightforward, but not simplistic, offering this refined muscle car in two distinct body styles. Buyers could select a stylish two-door hardtop coupe or an elegant convertible. Underneath, it featured heavy-duty suspension, upgraded shocks, beefy torsion bars, and standard hood scoops to match.
The standard engine for the 1967 Plymouth GTX was the formidable 440 cubic-inch Super Commando V8, introduced a year prior, foreshadowing the undisputed king off the ChryCo motor universe, the 426 Street Hemi.
Photo: Craigslist This massive powerplant generated a solid 375 horsepower and 480 lb-ft of torque. It allowed the heavy bruiser to accelerate from 0 to 60 mph in just 6.6 seconds. The quarter-mile was dispatched in 15.2 seconds at 97 mph, providing street credibility right off the showroom floor.
For the uncompromising speed enthusiasts, Plymouth offered the legendary 426 Hemi V8 engine as the sole available upgrade to the 440-cuber. This competition-derived elephant motor produced an astounding 425 horsepower and 490 lb-ft of torque (or so Plymouth claimed, but they downplayed it shamelessly).
A period road test of the 440 GTX by Car Life magazine from 1967 revealed a shockingly good piece of news: the standard 1967 GTX was actually quicker than the 1966 Hemi Satellite up until 90 mph. after that, the Hemi simply walked the 440 all over. So imagine what the Hemi GTX was capable of.
Photo: Craigslist Overall production numbers for the 1967 Plymouth GTX reached 12,690 units, with the vast majority being hardtops, with 12,010 examples rolling off the assembly line. The convertible variant was ordered in a scant 680 units. Because the 426 Hemi engine was a massively expensive upgrade, very few buyers stepped up to pay the extra $546 over the base $3,178 sticker price for the hardtop.
Most historical registries agree that a mere 125 examples of the 1967 Plymouth GTX left the factory equipped with the mighty 426 Hemi . That means the remaining 12,565 vehicles were powered by the standard 440 V8. Among the Hemi production run, experts note that 108 were hardtops and just 17 were convertibles. The transmission breakdown for those Hemi hardtops indicates 48 featured the TorqueFlite automatic, while 60 received manual gearboxes (4-speeds, how else?).
While official figures can occasionally vary, the broader automotive consensus states that 1,136 Hemi-powered Mopars were produced during 1967. This overall total surprisingly includes 720 units of the Plymouth GTX, 283 examples of the Dodge Coronet R/T, and 118 units of the Dodge Charger. Additional rare vehicles included six Plymouth Belvederes, another six Satellites, and three Dodge Coronets (non R/Ts).
Photo: Craigslist The GTX took no prisoners when it arrived, albeit its victory would be a short-lived triumph. Only a season later, in 1968, when it got the promotion to standalone model, it had to face the dreadful capitalist reality of “money talking,” when the Road Runner came about, and swept the GTX – and everyone else – off their feet. By 1971, the GTX was no longer financially viable, so Plymouth kicked it off the spotlight without remorse, demoting it to an engine package on the Road Runner.
Today, these incredibly scarce machines represent the absolute pinnacle of golden era classic performance. They typically take center stage at events like Mecum auctions or similarly scaled car events. However, there’s never a short supply of surprise in the automotive universe.
One of those gentleman's muscle car recently surfaced on Craigslist, looking for a new caretaker. Inspecting the weathered metal fender tag unlocks the factory specifications of this beast. It was scheduled for production on September 20, 1966, with a striking Bright Red exterior finish, premium black vinyl bucket seat interior. It rode on 7.75 x 14 Red Streak tires, with front disc brakes, an AM radio, and a cabin heater.
Photo: Craigslist The owner explicitly points out that the massive engine block has no repairs, sleeves, or hidden damage, running great after a rebuild that saw it punched out by 0.030 inches. It reportedly produces roughly 490 horsepower and 500 lb-ft on the dyno, offering a slightly more thrilling and realistic grunt than the original factory rating.
The odometer displays a remarkably low 23,000 miles, which is quite unusual for a vintage performance machine. The rust-free trunk pan and solid underside reflect a lifetime of careful preservation. The story goes that this car was a dragstripper back in the day, but the present owner doesn’t know how long that career lasted for.
To make room for the bigger, meaty rear rubbers, the wheel well lips were cut up, but that’s the only deviation from factory stock. The seats are something the seller takes little pride in, but the rest of the all-original interior is held in higher regard. He does have the covers and the foam to make the seats nice again, but that’s most probably a matter that a future owner will address.
This 1967 Plymouth GTX comes with a clean title and turn-key driver status, although a restoration is not excluded, if a purist if willing to pay the asking price of $74,500. The muscle car is located in Ashville, New York, but the seller mentions it originally came from the east coast (which probably explains the lack of rust).

Corvid Technologies plans to invest $95 million in a North Carolina expansion that will create 423 jobs and add a 400,000-square-foot manufacturing facility. The defense contractor will build the facility at its Mooresville headquarters to expand engineering and production of vehicle launch systems, Gov. Josh Stein announced earlier this week.
What’s Related
“In just two and a half years, we’ve grown from 8,000 square feet of manufacturing space to 800,000 square feet,” said Corvid President and CEO David Robinson. He said the company’s growth reflects demand from its customers.
The new jobs will include assemblers, electricians, engineers, production managers, technicians and testers. Annual salaries will average $81,550, compared with Iredell County’s average wage of $64,895, according to the state.
RELATED STORIES: Caterpillar Plans $1 Billion Manufacturing Push in North Carolina | Amazon, Corning Bring Massive Fiber Expansion to North Carolina
A new factory in Mooresville
Corvid plans to complete the new facility by the end of 2030, according to Business North Carolina . The company already has 382 workers in Mooresville and plans to add the new positions over the next four years.
Founded in 2004 as a small modeling and simulation firm, Corvid now works on projects ranging from missile launch systems to NASCAR. Its work includes design, prototyping, testing, and manufacturing.
The company considered Huntsville, Alabama, and Batavia, Ohio, before choosing Mooresville. Available workers, incentives, and infrastructure were among the factors in its decision, according to local reporting.
State incentives tied to hiring and investment
North Carolina’s Economic Investment Committee approved a grant that could reimburse Corvid up to $4,449,750 over 12 years. Payments will depend on state officials verifying that the company meets its annual hiring and investment targets.
Mooresville and Iredell County also committed a combined $6.4 million in property tax incentives, Business North Carolina reported. The company will receive $900,000 in workforce training.
The new agreement follows Corvid’s termination of a 2018 state incentive deal in September. The company repaid $126,745 in grants after telling the state it could not meet the earlier agreement’s hiring targets. Repaying that money was a condition of qualifying for the new grant, according to Business North Carolina.

Venti Technologies plans to introduce driverless container -moving trucks at a U.S. intermodal rail yard in 2026, beginning a rollout that could put more than 130 autonomous vehicles at eight railroad sites by 2027. The Boston-based company announced the planned launch Oct. 1 but has not named the railroad or the first location.
What’s Related
The trucks will move shipping containers inside operating rail yards, where freight transfers between trucks and trains. Venti says its vehicles can work alongside cranes, forklifts, trains, and human-driven trucks without dedicated lanes or changes to the terminal.
The rollout follows a long-term commercial agreement announced in July with an unnamed Class I North American railroad. That agreement includes potential expansion to more than 600 vehicles by the end of the decade, although Venti has not disclosed how many trucks will initially enter service.
Venti describes the planned deployment as North America’s first autonomous truck fleet for an intermodal rail yard. The company said it would provide more details in the coming weeks, but its announcement did not include an exact launch date.
Trucks operating through a busy yard
The planned trucks will operate without drivers on board, using Venti’s software to navigate through live yard traffic. The company says its vehicles handle positioning and driving decisions on board and can operate day and night, including in rain, snow and other bad weather.
Customers can use newly produced trucks or retrofit existing vehicles with Venti’s technology .
Although Venti describes the trucks as loading, moving, and unloading containers, it did not explain which loading tasks the vehicles perform or how they coordinate with container-handling equipment.
Experience in Singapore
Venti points to its work at PSA Singapore as evidence that its technology can handle busy freight operations. The company says its autonomous trucks have operated around the clock in full commercial production there for nearly three years, working among 1,200 human-driven trucks.
According to Venti, its vehicles have moved more than 360,000 containers in Singapore. The company also reports more than 500,000 autonomous miles across its fleet with no critical incidents, although the announcement did not define that term or provide an independent safety assessment.

When no suitable vessel was available to carry its gas turbine generators from the U.S. to Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea coast, the Rabigh Reinforcement project team turned to the heavy-lift charter market at a time when shipping conditions were already challenging. Drawing on its logistics experience and global agreements, the consortium engaged one of the world’s largest shipping carriers, which moved all the gas turbine generator bodies together on a single chartered vessel making a dedicated voyage to Saudi Arabia.
That kind of logistics improvisation is one example of how the 1,179-MW combined cycle plant reached first fire in July 2025 , roughly 14 months after the engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) contract was awarded. The project’s contracting structure, in which site preparation began in July 2023 and the contract was not awarded until May 2024, made that pace possible. But two executives responsible for delivering the plant say the schedule was protected by decisions made in the field: early planning, a deliberately built workforce, and a safety culture that kept 12 million man-hours free of lost-time injuries. Sandeep Kumar Gupta, sales director with Siemens Energy Gas Services, and Naira Elsayed, a senior project manager with Elsewedy Electric Power Systems Projects (PSP), described those decisions as guests on The POWER Podcast .
Early Alignment Protected the Schedule Before Contract Award
For roughly 10 months, early execution activities progressed while broader contractual and commercial arrangements were still being finalized. Gupta called the arrangement “certainly unconventional,” saying it worked only because of trust, alignment, and disciplined risk management among the three parties. The Saudi Electricity Company (SEC) accelerated bid evaluation and established interim mechanisms, including a limited notice to proceed and advance project payments, which allowed the consortium to order critical long-lead equipment and prepare the site.
Elsayed said the project management team also did something not normally done: It joined the proposal team during tendering to turn the project scope into an execution plan. “We took the tendering phase to plan our job and make ourselves ready for execution,” she said. Work on long-lead items began before the contract was signed.
When Red Sea Shipping Was Disrupted
Red Sea shipping disruption hit the project’s heaviest equipment, some of it coming from the U.S. The gas turbine generators charter protected the simple cycle milestone, but the steam turbine generator proved harder to move. Because it was a single unit, Elsayed said, chartering a dedicated vessel for it was difficult. Rather than wait, the team rerouted the 380-ton generator around the Cape of Good Hope to a port on the Arabian Gulf, far from the site. From there it spent 32 days on the road, a journey that required special permits, road modifications, and bridge adjustments that were not part of the original plan. “We cannot always control the external events, but we can control our response through flexibility, quick decisions, and strong partnership with alternative solutions,” she said.
Building a Workforce Ahead of Demand
Skilled labor was among the project’s biggest challenges, Elsayed said, because many large projects were running in parallel across Saudi Arabia under Vision 2030. Planning began during tendering, when the team ran a market survey to build a database of the manpower it would need. It then set up a small training and testing center at the site for welders and electrical technicians, and developed competitive employment packages.
The team also selected 25 fresh-graduate engineers from 100 applicants and enrolled them in a two-year training program, with the aim of placing them on the client side in plant operations. Work was divided into packages that experienced subcontractors with available crews could take on, and sister companies took some packages because of their capacity to supply manpower. Elsayed said her company’s reputation for moving good performers between projects helped retain them by offering “a career path, not just a job.”
Safety as Shared Responsibility
The project recorded no lost-time injuries even as its workforce peaked at about 2,500 people on site. Elsayed said the project had the standard elements of a strong safety program, including a professional safety team, continuous induction and training for subcontractors, and close monitoring of site activity. She said the difference was culture, built around the concept “that safety was everyone’s responsibility, not only the safety team.”
Safety performance was linked to key performance indicators across project roles, and subcontractors with strong records received recognition. The safety team also worked side by side with subcontractors to find safe alternatives “rather than simply reject unsafe works,” she said, so that work could proceed under high safety measures.
One Team, With a Track Record
Gupta said the partnership came down to clear roles, trust, and a shared goal. Siemens Energy delivered the power island, Elsewedy Electric PSP delivered the balance of plant and site execution, and SEC provided leadership as owner. “When issues came up, people picked up the phone and solved them rather than escalating them,” he said. Siemens Energy’s expansion beyond its traditional original equipment manufacturer (OEM) role into greater EPC responsibility, he added, helped streamline decision-making and reduce interfaces.
The partnership was already well established. Siemens (now Siemens Energy) and Elsewedy Electric previously delivered Beni Suef, one of three plants in Egypt’s 14.4-GW Megaproject , which POWER named its 2019 Plant of the Year. As a result, Elsayed said, the two companies did not need time to learn to work together at Rabigh, and their experience on many joint projects allowed execution to proceed smoothly.
Gupta was careful not to draw overly broad conclusions from the project. Whether Siemens Energy takes on a similar EPC role elsewhere will depend on the customer, the project requirements, and the risk profile, he said, and Rabigh should be viewed in the context of the specific needs of the project “rather than as a universal delivery model.” What he said is transferable is early alignment: Time at Rabigh was gained by getting the owner and the EPC partner aligned early on objectives, roles, and decision-making, and Siemens Energy is bringing that approach to other projects.

First-Ever BMW X9 Wants To Be the Cadillac Escalade’s Worst Nightmare – Rendering
11 photos
Photo: Behance | Noah Loemba
Did you think that BMW cannot possibly expand its crossover portfolio anymore? After all, it comprises all designations from the X1 premium subcompact model to the X7 flagship high-rider, and it also includes the XM, which is part of the M Division’s lineup.
Well, the logical answer would be no. Unless they somehow planned an X0.5. However, as it turns out, the answer is actually yes. You see, the X7 was deemed too small by the company’s US dealers, who want an even larger SUV. This model would obviously sit at the very top of the automaker’s portfolio, and would battle it out with the likes of the Cadillac Escalade and the Lincoln Navigator.
The latest Escalade measures up to 227 inches (5,766 mm) in length, and has a 134.1-inch (3,406 mm) long wheelbase in the ESV configuration. The fifth-gen Navigator measures up to 221.9 inches (5,636 mm) from bumper to bumper, and has 131.5 inches (3,340 mm) between the axles. As for the X7, it is 204 inches (5,181 mm) long, and has a wheelbase length of 122.2 inches (3,105 mm). Therefore, there is indeed room in BMW’s portfolio for an even larger crossover .
BMW’s dealers are now forcing the company to do something about it, reports indicate, and while technically the X7 does indeed qualify as a full-size SUV, it is obviously smaller than the Cadillac Escalade and the Lincoln Navigator. This is hardly official confirmation that such a thing is indeed coming, though it is plenty for the rendering crowd to go wild, which is why we have seen quite a few CGI takes on a hypothetical BMW X9 so far.
Photo: Behance | Noah Loemba Our latest encounter with such a thing came from Noah Loemba on Behance, and you can see the project in the photo gallery above. This thing does not exactly look like an enlarged X7 . In fact, it features a different front fascia with traditional headlights that are on the very slim side of things, yet they still manage to incorporate the daytime running lights. The bumper is also new, whereas the kidney grille is quite similar to that of the X7.
Further back, we can see a very clean design, not only for the front fenders, doors, and rear three-quarter panels, but also for the side glass, which almost looks like a canopy from certain angles. The taillights do not have anything to do with those of the X7, and the same goes for the tailgate, which features a split-opening design, and the rear bumper and diffuser. The wheels are on the large side of things, and they sport a familiar pattern.
The pixel artist has gone the extra mile by also imagining the interior of this rendered BMW X9 . And it looks pretty much the same as that of the X7. It has the same dashboard panel, and dual-screen setup, though there are a few differences, like the center console, new two-spoke steering wheel, buttons, knobs, and so on.
Mind you, if BMW will really give the X9 the green light for production, then its interior will be Neue Klasse. This means the Panoramic iDrive display from one pillar to the other at the bottom of the windshield, as well as the same infotainment system as the one seen on the new X5, among other models. Sure, it could spice things up with a few dedicated features, including perhaps upholstery and trim, but it likely won’t evade the Neue Klasse trend.
Photo: Behance | Noah Loemba After all, this is the recipe behind the upcoming BMW X7 , because the current flagship SUV is being replaced by an entirely new generation. And quite strangely (and fortunately, for that matter), it won’t go down the Neue Klasse route when it comes to the exterior design. This means that it will feature a front fascia that looks like an evolution of the current one, and that’s great news to our ears.
The back end should feature significantly larger taillights, and there will probably no longer be a split-opening tailgate. After all, the new X5 has lost this party trick, and we wouldn’t be surprised to learn that the future X7 will do that too. Thus, chances are that the first-ever X9 might look like an enlarged next-gen X7 on the outside, save for a few bits and bobs, and could get a very familiar-looking cockpit layout.
Word on the street is that the BMW X9 might launch in 2029 or maybe 2030, and an Alpina version could be part of the lineup to fight the Lincoln Navigator Black Label. But could there also be an X8 in BMW’s future portfolio? It’s a little too early to speak about that, but if we were to guess, we’d say that it could.
Now, before moving on to the next topic, what do you feel about an X9? And do you like the one signed by the quoted rendering artist ?

Photo: Ørsted
Revolution Wind is already sending electricity to New England, and all 65 turbines are installed. Now the Trump administration is challenging the federal approval that allowed the offshore wind farm to be built. Again. Yes, really.
The Interior Department asked a federal court on October 9 to send the project’s construction and operations plan approval back to the agency for reconsideration. The request creates another hurdle for a 704-megawatt (MW) wind farm that’s already survived two Trump administration attempts to stop construction.
But the DOI’s filing hasn’t stopped the turbines or revoked the offshore wind farm’s permit. The DOI’s request has to go to court, and Revolution Wind is expected to reach full commercial operation later this year.
A third attack on an approved project
The latest move comes as part of an ongoing lawsuit filed in 2024 by the anti-wind group Green Oceans, which challenged federal approvals for Revolution Wind and the nearby South Fork Wind project.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Trump’s Interior now wants to reconsider whether Revolution Wind’s approval complied with the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act. Its filing argues that the original decision didn’t adequately explain how the project’s impacts fit with protections for other ocean uses, including fishing and recreation, according to CT Mirror .
This is a completely different argument from the national security concerns the administration previously used to try to halt offshore wind construction.
Interior ordered work stopped at Revolution Wind in August 2025, then targeted it again in December alongside four other offshore wind projects. Court injunctions allowed construction to resume.
In a statement reported by CT Mirror , Interior said it was “complying with a briefing schedule, not announcing a policy change.” (Yeah, I don’t know what that word jumble means, either.)
Connecticut fights back
Connecticut officials responded on October 14, warning that reopening approvals undermine the certainty needed to build new electricity supplies.
Governor Ned Lamont (D-CT) said the action completely contradicts the Trump administration’s stated support for permitting reform aimed at speeding up energy projects and lowering costs. He said Connecticut is reviewing its options with Ørsted and the state attorney general’s office.
“This makes zero sense,” Attorney General William Tong said, adding that the state is prepared to return to court to defend the project.
There are electricity bills at stake, too. Connecticut’s Department of Energy and Environmental Protection estimates that, by 2028, Revolution Wind will reduce wholesale electricity market costs for New England ratepayers by about $500 million annually.
The $6.2 billion project began delivering electricity on March 13, 2026. Its developers say it will produce enough electricity for more than 350,000 homes and businesses, with power sold to Connecticut and Rhode Island utilities under fixed-price, 20-year agreements.
For now, the next decision rests with US District Judge Royce Lamberth – the same judge who twice allowed Revolution Wind’s developers to resume work after the administration tried to halt the offshore wind farm’s progress.
Electrek’s take
In September 2025 , the first time Reagan-appointed Judge Lamberth cleared the way for Revolution Wind to restart construction, he called the Trump government’s conduct “the height of arbitrary and capricious government conduct.”
In January 2026 , Judge Lamberth used the same words again, calling the Interior’s suspension order of Revolution Wind “arbitrary and capricious,” and said it was in violation of federal law.
This time, that wind farm is already powering the grid, and during an energy crisis brought about by Trump’s actions in the Middle East, no less. Lamberth’s decision will be impactful.

The tentative deal followed last-minute talks after earlier negotiations failed. ( Image: Screenshot from TRT World | YouTube )
Posted By: Cecilia Jamasmie October 14, 2026
BHP (ASX, LSE: BHP) and the supervisors’ union at its Escondida mine in Chile have reached a preliminary agreement to avert a strike at the world’s largest copper operation.
Members of Union No. 2 will vote online on the mining company’s latest proposal between 9:15 a.m. and 11:30 a.m. local time. If they reject it, the work stoppage would begin on Thursday at 8:00 a.m. loca time, newspaper La Tercera reported .
The tentative agreement emerged from last-minute negotiations after earlier contract talks failed to produce a deal.
The prospect of a shutdown had supported copper prices amid concerns that lost production at Escondida could tighten global supplies. A ratified agreement would remove one immediate threat to output, although Chile’s copper industry faces mounting operational and environmental risks.
Mounting disruptions
Labour disputes, operational setbacks and extreme weather linked to a stronger-than-expected El Niño are testing Chile’s copper producers, adding uncertainty to supply forecasts as analysts question the sustainability of recent price gains.
A deadly landslide at Codelco’s El Teniente mine over the weekend halted production at an open-pit section of the operation. El Teniente is the world’s largest underground copper mine and the state-owned producer’s biggest operation.
The incident adds to concerns highlighted in an early October study by GEM Mining Consulting, which estimated that an average 5.2% of production at Chile’s largest copper mines was vulnerable to strikes, severe weather, accidents and geological problems.
Riskiest operations
GEM’s Production-at-Risk Index assessed 14 major copper operations against eight threats, assigning risk scores ranging from 2.6% to 9%.
El Teniente ranked as the most exposed operation, with 9% of production at risk, followed by Los Pelambres at 8% and Escondida at 7.5%. Nine of the mines assessed had at least one threat classified as high risk.
The findings suggest that even if Escondida’s tentative labour deal is ratified, Chilean copper production remains vulnerable to disruptions beyond collective bargaining.

WASHINGTON — US Northern Command’s (NORTHCOM) task force for coordinating Golden Dome homeland air and missile defense capabilities across the Joint Force has been newly charged with enabling related cyberwar capabilities, according to a senior official.
Col. Kevin “Stoney” Stonerook, deputy commander of Joint Task Force-Gold (JTF-Gold), told reporters here today at the annual Association of the US Army conference that cyber warfare “has become a new mission set for us.”
“We are helping put together the team of teams, all the different stakeholder communities — be that vendors and other government agencies — to really provide a cyber warfare capability for GDA, and that’s one of the main things that we’re really focused on,” he said.
In later comments to Breaking Defense, however, Stonerook stressed that task force’s cyber activities were focused only on defense against adversary attacks on Golden Dome capabilities, rather than offensive activities.
NORTHCOM announced JTF-Gold with little fanfare, and almost no information, in January. The announcement noted that the head of Army Space and Missile Defense Command (SMDC) — a position held since April by Lt. Gen. John Rafferty — would be double-hatted as leader of the the task force, and co-located with SMDC at Peterson SFB, Colo.
“This new command enhances the integration and synchronization of the homeland’s integrated air and missile defense (IAMD) enterprise,” the announcement said.
Stonerook explained that JTF-Gold was created “out of the ashes” of US Space Command’s former Joint Force Component Command for Integrated Missile Defense. That component command’s mission “was really to take all things … of the missile defense system and make sure that that was well coordinated and orchestrated across the joint force,” he said.
“JTF-Gold was stood up to operationalize Golden Dome for America (GDA) for USNORTHCOM,” Stonerook said, and now sports about 100 personnel.
One of the the task force’s first missions has been to help develop “some of the sites as we look at building out GDA across the country and other areas, and trying to integrate all those capabilities across the multiple layers of GDA,” he said.
Stonerook said JTF-Gold was involved in siting and construction activities for Golden Dome’s first operational site at Fort Story, Va ., and will do the same at all future sites.
“But there’s a lot we still have to figure out,” he acknowledged.
For example, Stonerook said, Space Command’s integrated missile defense component command managed “all the assets across the missile defense system.” But now that JTF-Gold is under NORTHCOM, there is a need to figure out how to split those responsibilities.
“So, we’re still waiting to see where everything is falling out and whether those is needed redundancies. But our team is responsible for asset management, but the clear delineation of which assets are included and not included has not been completed.”
To that end, Stonerook said, JTF-Gold held a large “planning sprint” in February.
“We had over 300 people join us in Colorado Springs as we got a team of teams together to really understand who was doing what across the entirety of the GDA stakeholder community, and it was really beneficial,” he said. “It really kick started some of the planning, and we were able to develop concept of operations and continue on with a lot of the planning with things that were questions that were unanswered.”
Stonerook said that the next such planning sprint will be at the end of the month, focused on figuring out the respective responsibilities of the three “major” operations centers for Golden Dome at Peterson, Schriever SFB, Colo., and Tyndall AFB, Fla.
“What those roles and responsibilities are and where those lines are drawn, where there’s necessary redundancy, is still an active discussion. So, the planning sprint that we have at the end of the month, that’s one of the main topics of things that we’re going to get after,” he said. “[W]ho should be doing what, are we resourced to do those things, and what additional capabilities are there?”
